Computer fundamentals:
# Computer fundamentals
## Hardware
The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions using the fetch–decode–execute cycle. It contains the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), the control unit (CU) and registers such as the program counter. Primary memory includes RAM, which is volatile, and ROM, which is non-volatile. Cache is small, fast memory close to the CPU. A GPU is a processor specialized for parallel tasks such as graphics.

## Data and logic
Data is stored in binary. Hexadecimal is base 16. Integers are stored using two's complement; characters using ASCII or Unicode. Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR) combine binary inputs; truth tables show their outputs. An operating system manages hardware and software resources.

## Key terms
CPU: the processor that executes instructions
Fetch–decode–execute cycle: the cycle the CPU uses to run instructions
RAM: volatile main memory
Cache: small, fast memory near the CPU
Two’s complement: a way of storing negative integers in binary
Logic gate: a circuit that combines binary inputs
Networks:
# Networks
## Network types
A network is a set of connected devices that share data. A LAN covers a small area; a WAN covers a large area. Network topologies include star and mesh. A client–server network has central servers; a peer-to-peer network has equal devices.

## Protocols and security
A protocol is a set of rules for communication, such as TCP/IP, HTTP and DNS. The TCP/IP model has application, transport, internet and network access layers. Data is sent in packets. Security measures include encryption, firewalls, authentication and VPNs. Symmetric encryption uses one key; asymmetric encryption uses a public and a private key.

## Key terms
Network: connected devices that share data
Protocol: rules for communication between devices
Packet: a unit of data sent over a network
Firewall: a system that filters network traffic
Encryption: encoding data so only authorized parties can read it
LAN: a local area network covering a small area
Databases:
# Databases
## Relational databases
A database is an organized collection of data. A relational database stores data in tables (relations) of rows (records) and columns (fields). A primary key uniquely identifies a record; a foreign key links to a primary key in another table. Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy, up to third normal form (3NF).

## SQL and integrity
SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to create, query and update databases, with commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Data integrity means data is accurate and consistent. Transactions follow ACID properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

## Key terms
Relational database: data stored in linked tables
Primary key: a field that uniquely identifies a record
Foreign key: a field linking to another table’s primary key
Normalization: organizing tables to reduce redundancy
SQL: the language used to query databases
ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability
Machine learning:
# Machine learning
## Machine learning
Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which systems learn patterns from data instead of following explicit rules. Supervised learning trains on labelled data, for tasks such as classification and regression. Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data, such as clustering. Reinforcement learning learns by rewards and penalties.

## Models and ethics
Training data is used to build a model; test data checks its accuracy. Overfitting is when a model fits training data too closely and performs poorly on new data. Neural networks are layers of connected nodes that learn weights. Ethical issues include bias in training data, privacy and accountability.

## Key terms
Machine learning: systems that learn patterns from data
Supervised learning: training on labelled data
Unsupervised learning: finding patterns in unlabelled data
Overfitting: a model fitting training data too closely
Neural network: layers of connected nodes that learn weights
Training data: data used to build a model
Computational thinking:
# Computational thinking
## Thinking skills
Computational thinking is solving problems in a way a computer can help with. Decomposition is breaking a problem into smaller parts. Pattern recognition is spotting similarities. Abstraction is removing unnecessary detail. Algorithmic design is creating step-by-step solutions.

## Algorithms
An algorithm is a finite set of instructions to solve a problem. Algorithms can be shown as pseudocode or flowcharts. Standard algorithms include linear search, binary search, bubble sort and selection sort. Big O notation describes an algorithm's efficiency, such as O(n) for linear search and O(log n) for binary search.

## Key terms
Decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller parts
Abstraction: removing unnecessary detail
Algorithm: a finite set of instructions to solve a problem
Binary search: searching a sorted list by halving it each time
Big O notation: a description of an algorithm’s efficiency
Pseudocode: a structured, language-independent way to write algorithms
Programming:
# Programming
## Basics
Programs use variables to store data, with data types such as integer, float, string and Boolean. Control structures are sequence, selection (if statements) and iteration (loops). Functions are reusable blocks of code that take parameters and can return values.

## Good practice
Arrays and lists store collections of data. Recursion is a function calling itself, with a base case to stop. Testing uses normal, boundary and erroneous data. Debugging finds and fixes errors: syntax errors, logic errors and runtime errors. Scope is the part of a program where a variable can be used.

## Key terms
Variable: a named store for data
Iteration: repeating code using a loop
Function: a reusable block of code
Recursion: a function calling itself
Boundary data: test data at the edge of the valid range
Logic error: an error where code runs but gives the wrong result
Object-oriented programming:
# Object-oriented programming
## Objects and classes
Object-oriented programming (OOP) organizes code into objects that combine data and behaviour. A class is a template for objects; an object is an instance of a class. Attributes store data; methods define behaviour. A constructor creates a new object.

## Principles
Encapsulation hides an object's data behind methods. Inheritance lets a class take on the attributes and methods of a parent class. Polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same method call in their own way. Aggregation and composition describe objects containing other objects. UML class diagrams show classes and their relationships.

## Key terms
Class: a template for creating objects
Object: an instance of a class
Encapsulation: hiding data behind methods
Inheritance: a class taking on a parent’s attributes and methods
Polymorphism: different classes responding to the same method in their own way
Constructor: a method that creates a new object
Abstract data types:
# Abstract data types
## ADTs
An abstract data type (ADT) is defined by its operations, not its implementation. A stack is last in, first out (LIFO), with push and pop. A queue is first in, first out (FIFO), with enqueue and dequeue. A linked list stores nodes that point to the next node.

## Trees and more
A binary search tree stores values so that the left child is smaller and the right child is larger, allowing fast search. Traversals are in-order, pre-order and post-order. A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function. A set stores unique values.

## Key terms
Abstract data type: a data type defined by its operations
Stack: a last in, first out structure
Queue: a first in, first out structure
Linked list: nodes that each point to the next
Binary search tree: a tree with smaller values left and larger right
Hash table: a structure mapping keys to values with a hash function
Paper 1:
# Paper 1
## The paper
Paper 1 assesses the concepts of computer science: computer fundamentals, networks, databases and machine learning, with an HL extension. Questions range from short definitions to extended responses on scenarios, including a case study at HL.

## How to answer
Learn precise definitions and use technical vocabulary. In extended responses, apply concepts to the scenario, explain trade-offs and justify recommendations. Command terms such as outline, explain, compare and evaluate show the depth needed.

## Key terms
Case study: a scenario studied in advance for the HL paper
Command term: a word showing the depth of answer needed
Trade-off: a balance between two competing factors
Outline: give a brief account
Paper 2:
# Paper 2
## The paper
Paper 2 assesses computational thinking and programming. You read, trace, write and correct code in Java or Python, and design algorithms.

## How to prepare
Practise tracing code with trace tables, writing standard algorithms from memory, and using OOP and data structures. Write code that is clear, uses meaningful names and handles edge cases. A trace table records the values of variables as code runs.

## Key terms
Trace table: a table recording variable values as code runs
Edge case: an unusual input at the limit of what is expected
Syntax: the rules of how code must be written
Dry run: working through code by hand
Computational solution:
# Computational solution
## The internal assessment
The computational solution is the internal assessment: you design, build and test a program that solves a real problem for a client or user. You document the planning, design, development, testing and evaluation.

## Doing it well
Define the problem and success criteria clearly. Plan with diagrams such as UML and flowcharts. Show the development with techniques such as OOP, data structures and algorithms, explaining your choices. Test against the success criteria and evaluate the solution with the user. Success criteria are measurable goals the solution must meet.

## Key terms
Success criteria: measurable goals a solution must meet
Client: the person the solution is made for
UML diagram: a diagram showing the design of a system
Evaluation: judging the solution against its success criteria
